analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal rule that nursing home nurse aides get state-approved training and testing.
analysis.headline: The bill to scrap nurse aide training rules never left House committees and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1987, federal law has required nursing homes that bill Medicare or Medicaid to make sure their nurse aides complete a state-approved training program and competency test before working more than four months. This bill would erase that requirement for both programs, retroactive to the 1987 law that created it. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referrals to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing facilities would gain if it passed: they could hire aides with no training and no competency evaluation, avoiding the cost and time of the 1987 requirement. The bill would have applied retroactively, wiping out the standard as if it had never been enacted in the 1987 budget law [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that a nurse aide complete a state-approved training or competency evaluation program before a Medicare- or Medicaid-certified nursing facility uses them for more than four months [S2].
Repeals the same rules in both the Medicare program (Section 1819) and the Medicaid program (Section 1919) of the Social Security Act [S3].
Takes effect retroactively, as if it were part of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1987, which created the training requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home residents, most of them elderly and paid for through Medicare and Medicaid, would bear the cost: aides could care for them without any verified training or skills testing. Aides themselves would lose the federally guaranteed pathway to state-approved training.

drawbacks.text: The core drawback is the bill's whole purpose: it eliminates the only federal guarantee that the aides who feed, bathe, and monitor nursing home residents have completed state-approved training and passed a competency evaluation [S2].
Because it takes effect retroactively to the 1987 law, it would unwind training rules that were already in force, not just block future ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings go to nursing facility operators, who would no longer pay for aide training or wait for competency evaluations. The cost is borne by residents, who would be cared for by staff whose skills are never verified, and by aides, who lose the training standard. The bill offered no offsetting protections, so whatever savings facilities captured came directly out of the federal guarantee of minimum care quality.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees in May and June 1989, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas introduced the bill on May 10, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees [S1].
On May 16, 1989, the Ways and Means Committee sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and on June 1, 1989, Energy and Commerce sent it to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill died in subcommittee when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home residents and the aides who care for them came out ahead, because the federal training and competency requirement stayed on the books. Nursing facility operators lost the chance to cut their training obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home residents and nurse aides

sides.party_line_note: The 13 cosponsors split roughly evenly between parties (7 Democrats, 6 Republicans), and no recorded opposition ever formed because the bill died without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill would have freed Medicare and Medicaid certified nursing homes from paying for state-approved aide training and competency evaluations, retroactively erasing a 1987 rule. Residents would be cared for by unverified staff so operators could spend less.
Aides would lose the federal requirement that facilities provide state-approved training and that aides pass a competency evaluation, removing both a skills credential and a job-quality standard.

industries.industry: State nurse aide training and competency evaluation programs
industries.note: States would no longer operate federally required training and testing programs for nursing home aides under Medicare and Medicaid.
